positions/covenant-theology/oneLine: Scripture is organised by God’s covenants: a covenant of works with Adam, broken by the fall, and one covenant of grace in Christ administered under the Law and under the gospel, so that the people of God is one in both testaments.
positions/covenant-theology/coreClaims/0: Adam was the federal head of humanity in a covenant of works (Gen 2:16–17; Hos 6:7; Rom 5:12–21).
positions/covenant-theology/coreClaims/1: After the fall God made a single covenant of grace, revealed progressively to Noah, Abraham, Moses and David, and fulfilled in the new covenant.
positions/covenant-theology/coreClaims/2: Christ fulfils the covenant of works for his people (active and passive obedience) and is mediator of the covenant of grace.
positions/covenant-theology/coreClaims/3: Israel and the Church are one people under different administrations; children of believers are included as members (hence infant baptism).
positions/covenant-theology/coreClaims/4: The moral law, summarised in the Decalogue, remains a rule of life; ceremonial laws are fulfilled and judicial laws expired with Israel’s polity.
positions/covenant-theology/origin: Rooted in Zwingli’s and Bullinger’s defence of infant baptism (Bullinger, De testamento, 1534) and Calvin’s one covenant in two administrations; the covenant of works appears in Ursinus (c.1562), Dudley Fenner (1585) and Robert Rollock (1596); codified in the Westminster Confession (1647) and systematised by Cocceius (1648), Witsius (1677) and Turretin.
positions/covenant-theology/strongestArg: It explains the unity of Scripture: the same gospel was preached to Abraham (Gal 3:8) and the same faith saved Old Testament believers (Heb 11).
The Adam–Christ parallel of Romans 5 implies representative ("federal") headship in a covenant arrangement.
It gives a principled account of which Old Testament laws continue (moral) and which do not (ceremonial, civil).
It provides a rich framework for assurance, sacraments and the family in the church.
positions/covenant-theology/strongestObj: Scripture never explicitly names a "covenant of works" or a single overarching "covenant of grace"; critics (including some Reformed theologians like John Murray and Karl Barth) call these theological constructs.
Dispensationalists charge it with spiritualising promises to Israel; Baptists and New Covenant theologians argue it underplays the newness of the new covenant (Jer 31:34: "they shall all know me").
The tripartite division of the law (moral, ceremonial, civil) is not drawn explicitly in Scripture (cf. James 2:10).
positions/covenant-theology/responses/0: Defenders reply that the substance of a covenant with Adam is present (parties, condition, sanction, promise) even without the word, and Hosea 6:7 may name it.
positions/covenant-theology/responses/1: They argue that the newness of the new covenant lies in its fuller administration and Spirit, not in a different people or way of salvation.
positions/covenant-theology/responses/2: The threefold division, they note, is ancient (Aquinas, ST I-II q.99) and reflects distinctions Scripture itself makes between sacrifice and mercy (Hos 6:6).
positions/covenant-theology/consequences: The theological framework of the Westminster Standards, Puritanism and much Presbyterian and Reformed Baptist theology (in a Baptist form in the 1689 Confession).
Grounds infant baptism in Presbyterian and Reformed churches.
Shaped Puritan social covenants and, some historians argue, Anglo-American constitutionalism.
positions/dispensationalism-israel-churc: Dispensationalism (classical and revised): Israel and the Church distinct
Classical dispensationalism
Scofieldian dispensationalism
Revised (normative) dispensationalism

God works in distinct dispensations and has two peoples: national Israel, whose land and kingdom promises will be literally fulfilled in a future millennium, and the Church, a heavenly people formed at Pentecost and to be raptured before the tribulation.
Consistent literal-grammatical interpretation, especially of prophecy.
A distinction between Israel and the Church: the Church is a "parenthesis" or mystery not foreseen in the Old Testament (Eph 3:5–6).
The Abrahamic, Davidic and new covenants include unconditional promises to ethnic Israel that will be fulfilled nationally.
The Mosaic law, including the Sabbath, is not binding on the Church as a rule of life; believers live under grace.
Pretribulational rapture and premillennial return (see eschatology).
Genesis 12:1–3; 15
2 Samuel 7:12–16
Daniel 9:24–27
Romans 11:25–29
Ephesians 3:1–12
Romans 6:14 ("not under the law, but under grace")

Formulated by John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren (1830s), spread through Bible and prophecy conferences, the Scofield Reference Bible (1909; 1917) and Dallas Theological Seminary (1924); systematised by Lewis Sperry Chafer and Charles Ryrie (Dispensationalism Today, 1965).
Lewis Sperry Chafer
Charles C. Ryrie
John F. Walvoord
J. Dwight Pentecost
Michael Vlach
God’s oaths to Abraham’s physical descendants are presented as unconditional and everlasting (Gen 17:7–8; Jer 31:35–37); spiritualising them threatens God’s faithfulness.
Romans 11 distinguishes "Israel" from the Gentiles even within the church age and foresees a future national salvation.
Acts 1:6–7 assumes a future restoration of the kingdom to Israel; Jesus corrects only its timing.
Taking prophecy literally gave many believers confidence in Scripture and an interpretive key accessible to lay readers.
Ephesians 2:14–16 says Christ made the two "one new man", breaking down the dividing wall; two peoples with two destinies seems to rebuild it.
The New Testament itself applies Old Testament Israel promises to the church (Acts 15:15–17 citing Amos 9; Heb 8 citing Jer 31).
Critics note its recent origin (1830s) and its political consequences in unconditional support for modern Israel, at times at the expense of Palestinian Christians.
Dispensationalists answer that unity in salvation (one body) does not erase ethnic and national distinctions or promises (Rom 11:1, 29).
They argue that the Church shares in Israel’s spiritual blessings without replacing Israel’s national ones; progressive dispensationalists further nuance the distinction.
They reply that novelty in systematisation does not imply novelty in its premillennial and philosemitic elements, which have early precedents.
Dominant framework of 20th-century American fundamentalism and evangelical Bible colleges and missions.
Foundation of Christian Zionism and of evangelical support for the State of Israel.
Popularised through prophecy literature (Hal Lindsey, Left Behind).
positions/progressive-dispensationalism/: Progressive dispensationalism
PD
Revised dispensationalism (third phase)

The dispensations are progressive stages of one redemptive plan; Christ’s Davidic kingdom is already inaugurated, the Church is a genuine but partial fulfilment of the new covenant, and national Israel still has a future in the consummated kingdom.
Christ already reigns on David’s throne at the right hand of God (Acts 2:30–36), inaugurating the kingdom.
The Church is not a parenthesis but the present form of the one kingdom, made up of Jews and Gentiles who share new-covenant blessings.
Israel and the nations remain distinct identities within the eschatological kingdom; ethnic Israel will be restored.
Prophecy can have "complementary" fulfilments without cancelling the original sense.
Romans 11:26–29
Revelation 21:24–26

Emerged from the Dispensational Study Group of the Evangelical Theological Society (from 1986); named in 1991 and set out in Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock, Progressive Dispensationalism (1993), and Robert Saucy, The Case for Progressive Dispensationalism (1993).
Craig A. Blaising
Robert L. Saucy
Mark Saucy
Peter’s Pentecost sermon identifies Christ’s exaltation with the fulfilment of the Davidic promise, which classical dispensationalism had postponed.
It honours both the unity of salvation (one new humanity) and the distinct future of Israel.
It narrows the gap with covenant theology while keeping exegetical commitments on Romans 11.
Classical dispensationalists (e.g. Ryrie, Robert Thomas) argue it abandons consistent literal interpretation and the Israel–Church distinction.
Covenant theologians reply that once the Davidic kingdom is inaugurated in the church, a further national phase looks redundant.
Its "complementary hermeneutic" can seem to allow both literal and spiritual readings as convenient.
Progressives answer that the New Testament itself shows "already/not yet" fulfilment, which a mature hermeneutic must follow.
They argue that Israel’s national restoration is required by the irrevocability of God’s promises (Rom 11:29) and by passages like Acts 3:19–21.
Now taught at Dallas Theological Seminary and Talbot alongside older forms.
Opened sustained dialogue with covenant theologians and progressive covenantalists.
positions/new-covenant-theology/oneLine: The whole Mosaic covenant, including the Ten Commandments as a covenant document, was fulfilled and ended in Christ; believers are under the new covenant and "the law of Christ", which includes those Old Testament commands the New Testament reaffirms.
positions/new-covenant-theology/coreClai: The Mosaic covenant is a unit; it cannot be divided into moral, ceremonial and civil parts.
Christ is the new lawgiver, and the New Testament is the Christian’s rule of life (1 Cor 9:21; Gal 6:2).
Nine of the Ten Commandments are restated in the New Testament; the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ’s rest (Heb 4).
The new covenant community is a regenerate people, so baptism is for believers only.
Rejects a "covenant of works" with Adam as an unbiblical construct.
positions/new-covenant-theology/origin: Developed among Reformed Baptists in the United States from the late 1970s and 1980s (John G. Reisinger, Jon Zens, Fred Zaspel, Tom Wells), drawing on earlier Baptist and Lutheran reservations about the third use of the Decalogue; set out in Wells and Zaspel, New Covenant Theology (2002).
positions/new-covenant-theology/stronges: Paul calls the covenant "written and engraven in stones", that is, the Decalogue, a ministry "done away" (2 Cor 3:7–11).
Scripture treats the Law as a single covenant: "whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all" (Jas 2:10).
It explains why the New Testament never commands Sabbath observance while repeating the other commandments.
Covenant theologians argue it risks antinomianism by detaching the moral law from creation and the Decalogue.
Critics say "the law of Christ" is underdefined and leaves ethical questions (e.g. on marriage and sexuality) with fewer Old Testament resources.
Its relative novelty and lack of confessional expression concern confessional Baptists who hold the 1689 Confession.
positions/new-covenant-theology/response: NCT proponents reply that the eternal moral will of God is not abolished but now known through Christ and the apostles, so the Old Testament remains profitable Scripture (2 Tim 3:16).
They argue that reading every command through Christ is more, not less, demanding (Matt 5:21–48).
positions/new-covenant-theology/conseque: A significant minority view among Reformed Baptists and some evangelical seminaries.
Sharpened debate about the Sabbath and the Decalogue in Baptist confessional circles.
